**Question.** On what were these numbers measured, and how are they reproduced?

**Result.** Everything was measured on one workstation with the production SGB core at one commit, on random layouts of seed 2. The measuring scripts write JSON data files; one plotting script turns those files into the figures and tables of this study.

## One caveat for all numbers

Each case ran once, on a workstation that was not isolated from other work: around the Gmsh API and validator runs its load average was between 1.6 and 3.5, and it was not recorded for the scaling run. Times measured in more than one run agree to within about 25% (the direct writer at 1,000 features: 0.35 s and 0.44 s; the Gmsh API at 2,000 features: 63.3 s and 64.7 s). The Gmsh API run at 2,000 features was repeated three times and the stored 64.7 s is the last; another job on the machine made the first take 83.6 s. Read the numbers for orders of magnitude and slopes, not for small differences between two cases.

## Machine

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| CPU | AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 9975WX, 32 cores, 2 threads per core, 1 socket (64 hardware threads) |
| Memory | 503 GiB |
| Operating system | Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, Linux kernel 6.8.0-138-generic, x86_64 |

## Software

| Item | Version |
|---|---|
| SGB core (`scgsim.geometry.sgb`, production package) | commit `c034f61` |
| Python | 3.12.14 |
| Gmsh (Python API) | 4.15.2 |
| OCP (`cadquery-ocp-novtk`, used by the OCCT checks) | 7.8.1.1.post1, on OCCT 7.8.1 |

## Layouts {#layouts}

The layout generator is `random_layout` of the SGB test suite (`tests/sgb_scenes.py`): N features on a square grid at a pitch of 260 µm, each in its own cutout of one ground plane, over a substrate and under a vacuum body, built with Route B. About a quarter of the features carry a second shape of the same Net that overlaps the first. Features are polygons; there are no circular arcs and no inset bands.

The seed is 2 throughout. Seed 1 is not used because at 20,000 features it draws two shapes of one Net (`f5879` and `f5879b`) that touch at a single vertex. The production build rejects such an input with `NonManifoldError`: a same-Net pinch is invalid by design, so the rejection is correct. Seeds 2 to 9 all build at 20,000 features.

The scaling run measures 1,000, 5,000 and 20,000 features, each in its own Python process so that peak memory belongs to that case. The Gmsh API comparison and the validator timings use 500, 1,000 and 2,000 features and 1,000, 5,000 and 20,000 features respectively.

## Data files

The files are stored with the SGB design pages, in `zh-TW/docs/design/sgb/figures/`.

| File | Holds | Written by |
|---|---|---|
| `why-scaling-measured.json` | one case per N: stage times, counts, peak memory, identity digest, the written files, the Gmsh load and `verify_loaded` | `why_scaling.py measure` |
| `why-scaling-oracle.json` | Gmsh API construction at 500, 1,000 and 2,000 features: times and solid masses | `why_scaling.py oracle` |
| `why-validator-scaling.json` | time of twelve structural checks at 1,000, 5,000 and 20,000 features; a second timing, not plotted here | `why_scaling.py validators` |
| `emission-timing-data.json` | Gmsh API against the direct writer, stage by stage, and the timing of every check (structural and on the loaded model) | `emission.py --measure` |
| `emission-example-numbers.json` | counts of the example model and the OCCT check timings on the test models | `emission.py` |

## Commands

Run from the repository root with the Python environment of an SGB core checkout at the commit above. `SGB_CORE` points to that checkout, which also holds the test builders the scripts import.

```bash
SGB_CORE=<SGB core checkout>
PY=<Python interpreter of the SGB core environment, with gmsh and OCP installed>
export SGB_CORE

$PY zh-TW/docs/design/sgb/_figures/why_scaling.py measure       # about 5 minutes
$PY zh-TW/docs/design/sgb/_figures/why_scaling.py oracle
$PY zh-TW/docs/design/sgb/_figures/why_scaling.py validators
$PY zh-TW/docs/design/sgb/_figures/emission.py --measure
```

The figures and tables of this study need only `matplotlib` and the JSON files. They are written for both languages by one script:

```bash
python3 docs/research/geometry-build/_figures/plots.py
```

The script writes the SVG figures and Markdown tables to `figures/` beside each language's pages, and `numbers.json` with the values the text quotes. Edit the data only by rerunning the measuring scripts; the plotting script holds no numbers.

The measuring scripts and their inputs are described in `zh-TW/docs/design/sgb/_figures/README.md`.
